notes: Community pack, roadmap Phase 1 candidate. 5 tracks x 10 themes x 5 grade bands = 250 blocks. Expanded by tools/generate_pack.py.

themes.theme: The risks where you actually live
themes.description: Flood maps, fault lines, storm tracks and the industrial site up the road — replacing generic fear with your address's real risk list.
themes.transfer_check: Build the ranked hazard list for your own address from official maps and records, with the evidence for each entry.

bands.K–2: With an adult, name the two things that could go wrong where you live — the big water, the big wind — and point to where you would go.
bands.3–5: Find your home on a printed flood or storm map with help, colour the risks that touch it, and list them from most to least likely.
bands.6–8: Look up the official hazard maps for your address yourself, list every risk that touches it, and say where each entry came from.
bands.9–10: Build the ranked hazard list for your address from official maps and records, with a source and a likelihood note on every entry.
bands.11–12: Build the ranked list for a household other than your own, defend the ranking to its members, and file the sources so they can check you.

themes.theme: Seventy-two hours on your own shelf
themes.description: Water, food, light, warmth, medication — the kit that keeps a household functional for three days, sized to the people actually in it.
themes.transfer_check: Assemble or audit a real 72-hour kit for your household's actual members, including the items lists always forget.

bands.K–2: Help gather the family's water, snacks, a light and a blanket into one box, and count the people the box is for.
bands.3–5: Write the three-day list for your own household — water by the person, food that needs no stove, light, warmth, medicine — and check the shelf against it.
bands.6–8: Audit the household's real kit against a three-day standard, find what is missing or expired, and make the replacement list with costs.
bands.9–10: Assemble or audit a complete 72-hour kit sized to the people, pets and prescriptions actually in the household, including the items lists forget.
bands.11–12: Size and assemble a kit for a household with a named special need — an infant, a dialysis patient, a wheelchair user — and write the rotation schedule.

themes.theme: The grab bag and the ninety seconds
themes.description: Documents, medications, chargers, cash — what leaves the house with you when there is no time to choose.
themes.transfer_check: Pack a real grab bag, stage it, and run the ninety-second evacuation drill with it twice.

bands.K–2: Practise the leave-now game: grab your own small bag with one comfort thing in it and get to the door with an adult before the count ends.
bands.3–5: Pack your own grab bag from a checklist — copies of your name card, a torch, a snack, a charger — and time yourself getting it to the door.
bands.6–8: Pack the household's grab bag with the documents, medicines, chargers and cash that leave with you, and run the ninety-second drill twice.
bands.9–10: Pack and stage a real grab bag for the whole household, run the ninety-second evacuation drill twice, and fix what the drill found slow.
bands.11–12: Design the grab-bag standard for a family other than your own — contents, staging point, who carries what — and run their first drill with them.

themes.description: The out-of-area contact, the rally points, and how a separated household finds itself when networks are down or jammed.
themes.transfer_check: Write your household's communication plan on one card per person and test it with an unannounced check-in drill.

bands.K–2: Learn the name and number of the grown-up who lives far away, and practise saying your own full name and street to an adult.
bands.3–5: Fill in the family contact card — the far-away person, the meeting place near home, the one farther out — and keep it in your bag.
bands.6–8: Write the household's communication plan, one card per person, with the out-of-area contact and two rally points, and hand the cards out.
bands.9–10: Write the household's communication plan on one card per person and test it with an unannounced check-in drill where no one is warned.
bands.11–12: Write and test the plan for a household that includes someone who cannot use a phone unaided, and record how the drill reached them.

themes.description: Storage amounts per person, the sources hiding in a home, and making questionable water drinkable.
themes.transfer_check: Locate and quantify every emergency water source in a real dwelling, and demonstrate one purification method correctly.

bands.K–2: Find where the family keeps spare water, and help pour and count enough bottles for everyone for one day.
bands.3–5: Work out how many litres your household needs for three days, count what is stored, and find one more place in the home that holds clean water.
bands.6–8: Find every emergency water source in your dwelling — tank, heater, ice, stored bottles — quantify each, and show one way to make doubtful water safe.
bands.9–10: Locate and quantify every emergency water source in a real dwelling and demonstrate one purification method correctly, stating its limits.
bands.11–12: Plan three days of water for a household of six from what the dwelling actually holds, demonstrate two purification methods, and say when each fails.

themes.description: Light, heat, cooking and phones through an outage — running the essentials safely without the grid, and the CO line never crossed.
themes.transfer_check: Run a two-hour household blackout drill covering light, one hot meal and phone charging, with every method used safely.

bands.K–2: Practise finding the torch in the dark, and learn the one rule: no fire or camp stove inside the house, ever.
bands.3–5: Help run a lights-out hour at home — torch, blankets, a cold meal — and say why the grill and the generator stay outside.
bands.6–8: Run a two-hour blackout drill at home covering light, one hot meal and phone charging, and name the carbon-monoxide line you never cross.
bands.9–10: Run a two-hour household blackout drill covering light, one hot meal and phone charging, with every method used safely and logged.
bands.11–12: Plan and run the blackout drill for a household with medical equipment or an infant, including the fallback for a device that needs power.

themes.description: IDs, deeds, policies, prescriptions — the copies, the cloud, the sealed pouch, and proving who you are when the originals burned.
themes.transfer_check: Create the full document backup for a real household — physical copies staged, digital copies encrypted and reachable.

bands.K–2: Draw or trace your name card and put a copy of it in the family's special pouch with an adult.
bands.3–5: Help make the list of the papers that matter — who we are, where we live, the doctor's notes — and put copies in a sealed bag.
bands.6–8: Make photocopies and photographs of the household's key documents, store the digital set with a password, and put the paper set in the grab bag.
bands.9–10: Create the full document backup for a real household — physical copies staged, digital copies encrypted and reachable — and test recovering one.
bands.11–12: Design the backup for a household that has just lost its originals, walking through how each identity is proven again, and write the recovery steps.

themes.theme: Pets and the beings who cannot pack
themes.description: Animals in evacuation: carriers, records, the shelters that take them and the ones that will not.
themes.transfer_check: Build the evacuation plan and kit for a real animal, and complete a timed load-and-go drill with it.

bands.K–2: Help put the pet's lead, a food scoop and its picture into one bag, and practise calling the animal calmly.
bands.3–5: Make the pet's own kit — food for three days, water, medicine, its records and photo — and practise getting it into its carrier.
bands.6–8: Build the evacuation plan and kit for a real animal, find the shelters that take it, and run a timed load-and-go drill with it.
bands.9–10: Build the evacuation plan and kit for a real animal, and complete a timed load-and-go drill with it, with the shelter and vet contacts confirmed.
bands.11–12: Plan the evacuation of animals for a household with more than one species or a large animal, including transport and the shelter that will refuse them.

themes.description: The street-level map of who has skills, tools and needs — preparedness as a shared asset rather than a private bunker.
themes.transfer_check: Map your immediate neighbours' relevant skills, equipment and vulnerabilities (with consent), and agree one mutual commitment.

bands.K–2: Name the neighbour a grown-up trusts, and practise knocking and asking for help politely.
bands.3–5: Draw your street and mark, with an adult, the houses of people who could help and people who might need help.
bands.6–8: Map your immediate neighbours' skills, equipment and needs with their consent, and agree one thing you will do for each other in an event.
bands.9–10: Map your immediate neighbours' relevant skills, equipment and vulnerabilities (with consent), and agree one mutual commitment in writing.
bands.11–12: Organise the street's mutual-aid map, host the conversation that gets consent, and write the one-page agreement the neighbours sign.

themes.description: Why untested plans fail, rotating supplies before they expire, and the twice-yearly hour that keeps readiness real.
themes.transfer_check: Run a full household drill against your written plan, log every failure found, and fix the worst one the same week.

bands.K–2: Practise the family drill once with the adults, and put a sticker on the calendar for the next time.
bands.3–5: Run the household drill with the family, write down one thing that did not work, and mark the next drill date on the calendar.
bands.6–8: Run a full household drill against the written plan, log every failure found, and fix the worst one in the same week.
bands.9–10: Run a full household drill against your written plan, log every failure found, and fix the worst one the same week, dated and signed.
bands.11–12: Design and run the twice-yearly drill cycle for a household or small group, including supply rotation, and write the after-action note others can use.

tracks.name: First aid: the first ten minutes

themes.description: Danger, response, airway — why rescuers become casualties, and the look-around that comes before the kneel-down.
themes.transfer_check: Approach three staged casualty scenes, verbalising the hazard check and the decision to proceed, stage, or wait for each.

bands.K–2: Learn to stop and look before running to help — cars, water, fire — and to fetch a grown-up first.
bands.3–5: Practise the look-around at three pretend scenes, say out loud what could hurt you, and decide whether to go closer or call for help.
bands.6–8: Approach three staged casualty scenes, say the hazard check aloud, and decide for each whether to proceed, stage back, or wait for help.
bands.9–10: Approach three staged casualty scenes, verbalising the hazard check and the decision to proceed, stage, or wait for each, with reasons.
bands.11–12: Run the scene check for a group of helpers at a staged incident, assign safe roles, and stop anyone about to become a second casualty.

themes.description: What the call-taker needs, in what order, and the location skills (addresses, apps, landmarks) that cut minutes off arrival.
themes.transfer_check: Complete a realistic mock emergency call scored against dispatch criteria, including conveying a precise location two ways.

bands.K–2: Practise saying your name, your street and what is wrong to a pretend call-taker, and know which number to press.
bands.3–5: Make a practice emergency call and give your address two ways — the street and a landmark — in the order the call-taker asks.
bands.6–8: Complete a realistic mock emergency call scored against dispatch criteria, giving the location two ways and answering the questions in order.
bands.9–10: Complete a realistic mock emergency call scored against dispatch criteria, including conveying a precise location two ways and staying on the line.
bands.11–12: Coach a novice through a mock emergency call while managing the scene, and debrief which of the call-taker's questions they missed.

themes.theme: The unconscious person who is breathing
themes.description: Checking response and breathing, the recovery position, and staying until handover.
themes.transfer_check: Demonstrate the full assessment and recovery position on a live volunteer, including the monitoring you keep doing.

bands.K–2: Practise gently shaking and calling a doll's name, then running to a grown-up when it does not answer.
bands.3–5: Practise checking whether a person answers and is breathing, and roll a partner onto their side the way you were shown.
bands.6–8: Demonstrate the response and breathing checks and the recovery position on a partner, and keep watching their breathing until told to stop.
bands.9–10: Demonstrate the full assessment and recovery position on a live volunteer, including the monitoring you keep doing until handover.
bands.11–12: Teach the assessment and recovery position to a small group, correct their errors, and manage a handover to a simulated ambulance crew.

themes.theme: CPR and the machine on the wall
themes.description: Compressions that are hard and fast enough, rescue breaths where trained, and using an AED with its voice as your guide.
themes.transfer_check: Perform two minutes of adequate-rate, adequate-depth compressions on a manikin and run a full AED sequence to shock/no-shock.

bands.K–2: Practise pushing hard on a doll's chest to a steady beat, and find the box on the wall with the heart picture.
bands.3–5: Practise chest pushes on a manikin at the right speed with a song to keep time, and point to where the AED lives in your building.
bands.6–8: Perform two minutes of compressions on a manikin at adequate rate and depth, and follow an AED trainer's voice through its sequence.
bands.9–10: Perform two minutes of adequate-rate, adequate-depth compressions on a manikin and run a full AED sequence to shock or no-shock.
bands.11–12: Lead a two-rescuer CPR cycle with a swap, run the AED, and coach a bystander to take over compressions without losing the rhythm.

themes.description: The universal sign, back blows and abdominal thrusts, and the differences for infants and the pregnant.
themes.transfer_check: Demonstrate the complete choking protocol on adult and infant manikins, adapting correctly for each.

bands.K–2: Learn the hands-at-the-throat sign and shout for a grown-up when you see it.
bands.3–5: Show the choking sign, and practise the back blows on a manikin the way you were shown.
bands.6–8: Demonstrate back blows and abdominal thrusts on an adult manikin, and show the differences for an infant.
bands.9–10: Demonstrate the complete choking protocol on adult and infant manikins, adapting correctly for each and for the pregnant.
bands.11–12: Assess and manage a staged choking casualty end to end, including the transition to CPR when they collapse, and teach the protocol to a novice.

themes.description: Pressure, elevation, packing and the tourniquet's honest place — stopping blood loss with what is in reach.
themes.transfer_check: Control three staged bleeds — minor, severe limb, junctional — choosing and applying the right technique for each.

bands.K–2: Practise pressing a clean cloth on a pretend cut and holding it still while a grown-up comes.
bands.3–5: Practise firm pressure with a pad on a staged cut, lift the limb, and keep pressing until told it has stopped.
bands.6–8: Control two staged bleeds — a minor cut and a severe limb wound — choosing pressure, packing or a tourniquet trainer and applying it correctly.
bands.9–10: Control three staged bleeds — minor, severe limb, junctional — choosing and applying the right technique for each, with times recorded.
bands.11–12: Manage a staged multiple-casualty bleed, prioritise, apply and document a tourniquet with its time, and hand over to a simulated crew.

themes.theme: Burns, breaks and the injuries that wait badly
themes.description: Cooling burns properly, immobilising suspected fractures, and the do-nots that make each worse.
themes.transfer_check: Manage one staged burn and one staged fracture end to end, stating what you will not do and why.

bands.K–2: Learn to run cool water over a small burn and to leave a hurt arm still until a grown-up comes.
bands.3–5: Cool a staged burn under running water for the right time, and keep a partner's pretend broken arm still with a cushion.
bands.6–8: Manage one staged burn and one staged fracture, saying what you will not do — no ice, no creams, no straightening — and why.
bands.9–10: Manage one staged burn and one staged fracture end to end, stating what you will not do and why, and improvising a splint.
bands.11–12: Manage a staged burn and fracture on a casualty who must be moved, deciding when moving is justified, and brief a crew on what was done.

themes.description: Heart attack, stroke, seizure, severe allergy, diabetic collapse — recognising each fast and the one right action for each.
themes.transfer_check: From five scripted casualty presentations, identify each condition and perform or state its correct first response, including auto-injector use.

bands.K–2: Learn what a grown-up looks like when very unwell, and practise fetching help and the family's medicine bag.
bands.3–5: Match five picture cards — chest pain, a drooping face, a fit, a swelling allergy, a shaky diabetic — to the one thing you do for each.
bands.6–8: From five scripted presentations, name each condition and state or perform its correct first response, including a trainer auto-injector.
bands.9–10: From five scripted casualty presentations, identify each condition and perform or state its correct first response, including auto-injector use.
bands.11–12: Run a scenario with two presentations at once, triage them, direct helpers, and give a structured handover naming each condition and the time.

themes.description: Children and infants: the doses, ratios and signs that differ, and keeping a frightened child workable.
themes.transfer_check: Adapt three adult protocols correctly to a child or infant manikin, and demonstrate one calming approach while treating.

bands.K–2: Practise being gentle with a baby doll and calling a grown-up when a small child is hurt.
bands.3–5: Practise the softer pushes and breaths for a baby manikin, and say one calm thing you would tell a frightened little one.
bands.6–8: Adapt three adult protocols to a child or infant manikin and demonstrate one way of calming a frightened child while treating.
bands.9–10: Adapt three adult protocols correctly to a child or infant manikin, and demonstrate one calming approach while treating.
bands.11–12: Manage a staged paediatric emergency with a distressed parent present, adapt the protocol, and direct the parent to a useful role.

themes.theme: The kit and the kit in your head
themes.description: Building a first-aid kit that matches your life, improvising when there is none, and the refresher rhythm that keeps skills alive.
themes.transfer_check: Assemble a first-aid kit for a named context (home, car, hike), justify every item, and treat one staged injury using improvised materials only.

bands.K–2: Find the first-aid box at home, and name three things inside and what they are for.
bands.3–5: Check the family first-aid kit against a picture list, and make a card of what is missing.
bands.6–8: Assemble a first-aid kit for one named place — home, car or hike — justify every item, and treat one staged injury with improvised materials only.
bands.9–10: Assemble a first-aid kit for a named context (home, car, hike), justify every item, and treat one staged injury using improvised materials only.
bands.11–12: Specify the kits for three contexts and a refresher calendar for a group, then run a drill where the kit is missing and only improvisation is allowed.

themes.theme: How fires actually start at home
themes.description: Cooking, smoking, chargers, candles, heaters — the ignition league table and the habits behind each entry.
themes.transfer_check: Audit a real dwelling against the top ignition causes and eliminate or mitigate every finding, with photos.

bands.K–2: Walk the home with an adult and point to the hot things — the stove, the heater, the candles — that are never touched alone.
bands.3–5: Make a picture list of the top ways home fires start and check your own home for each one with an adult.
bands.6–8: Audit your own home against the top ignition causes, fix or flag every finding, and photograph the before and after.
bands.9–10: Audit a real dwelling against the top ignition causes and eliminate or mitigate every finding, with photos and a dated record.
bands.11–12: Audit a dwelling you do not live in, present the findings to its occupants in their own priorities, and agree the fixes and the dates.

themes.theme: The alarms that buy the minutes
themes.description: Smoke and heat detector types, where each belongs, and the dead battery that undoes it all.
themes.transfer_check: Verify correct type, placement and function of every alarm in a real dwelling, and fix or specify what is missing.

bands.K–2: Learn the sound of the smoke alarm and practise what you do when you hear it: get out, stay out.
bands.3–5: Find every alarm in your home with an adult, press the test buttons, and mark on a drawing where they are.
bands.6–8: Verify the type, placement and function of every alarm in your home, and list what is missing or in the wrong place.
bands.9–10: Verify correct type, placement and function of every alarm in a real dwelling, and fix or specify what is missing.
bands.11–12: Specify the alarm scheme for a dwelling with a deaf or heavy-sleeping occupant — types, placement, interlinking — and verify the installation.

themes.theme: The escape plan with two ways out
themes.description: Routes, the smoke-low crawl, the closed-door discipline and the meeting point nobody re-enters from.
themes.transfer_check: Draw the two-route escape plan for a real dwelling and run the drill with its actual occupants, timed, including the meeting point.

bands.K–2: Practise the crawl-low-and-go from your bedroom to the door, and the meeting place outside the family chose.
bands.3–5: Draw your home with two ways out of your room, mark the meeting place, and run the escape with the family once.
bands.6–8: Draw the two-route escape plan for your home, run the timed drill with its real occupants, and end at the meeting point.
bands.9–10: Draw the two-route escape plan for a real dwelling and run the drill with its actual occupants, timed, including the meeting point.
bands.11–12: Write and drill the escape plan for a dwelling with an upper floor and a mobility-impaired occupant, and fix the route the drill proved unusable.

themes.theme: Fighting the small fire, fleeing the rest
themes.description: Extinguisher classes, the pan fire and the fire blanket, and the honest size limit where fighting stops and leaving starts.
themes.transfer_check: Match extinguisher types to five fire scenarios, demonstrate the technique (live or simulated), and state your personal stop-and-go line.

bands.K–2: Learn that children never fight fires: get out and tell a grown-up.
bands.3–5: Learn the picture labels on extinguishers and say which fire — paper, oil, electric — each is for, and when everyone just leaves.
bands.6–8: Match extinguisher types to five fire scenarios and demonstrate the technique on a trainer or simulator, then state your own stop-and-go line.
bands.9–10: Match extinguisher types to five fire scenarios, demonstrate the technique (live or simulated), and state your personal stop-and-go line.
bands.11–12: Run a fire-blanket and extinguisher station for others, correct their technique, and enforce the size limit where fighting stops and leaving starts.

themes.description: What smoke does in minutes, why closed doors matter for hours, and surviving in a room you cannot leave.
themes.transfer_check: Demonstrate the trapped-in-room protocol — door checks, sealing, the window signal, the call — in a staged scenario.

bands.K–2: Practise staying low under pretend smoke and closing the door behind you.
bands.3–5: Practise the closed-door test — the back of the hand on the door — and what to do if it is hot: stay, seal, signal.
bands.6–8: Demonstrate the trapped-in-room protocol in a staged scenario — door check, sealing the gap, the window signal, the call.
bands.9–10: Demonstrate the trapped-in-room protocol — door checks, sealing, the window signal, the call — in a staged scenario, with a partner timing you.
bands.11–12: Teach the trapped-in-room protocol to a class, run the staged scenario for them, and debrief the one step they most often skip.

themes.theme: The building bigger than your door
themes.description: Apartment blocks: stay-put versus evacuate policies, alarm systems, dry risers and why the policy differs by construction.
themes.transfer_check: Find and explain your own building's fire strategy, and state exactly what you would do for an alarm at 3 a.m. under it.

bands.K–2: Learn what the alarm in a big building sounds like and follow the grown-up to the outside meeting place.
bands.3–5: Find the escape signs and the fire doors in your school or building, and walk the route to the assembly point.
bands.6–8: Find and explain your own building's fire strategy — stay put or evacuate — and say what you would do for an alarm at three in the morning.
bands.9–10: Find and explain your own building's fire strategy, and state exactly what you would do for an alarm at 3 a.m. under it, with the reasons.
bands.11–12: Compare the fire strategies of two buildings of different construction, explain why they differ, and write the resident notice for one of them.

themes.theme: Wildfire at the edge of town
themes.description: Ember attack, defensible space, the leave-early principle and the go/no-go decision made before smoke is visible.
themes.transfer_check: Assess a real or case-study property's wildfire exposure, specify its defensible-space actions, and write its trigger-based leave plan.

bands.K–2: Learn the go-early rule: when the grown-ups say we leave, we leave, before the smoke.
bands.3–5: Look at a house at the edge of the trees on a picture or map and name three things around it that could burn.
bands.6–8: Assess a real or case-study property's wildfire exposure and list its defensible-space actions in order.
bands.9–10: Assess a real or case-study property's wildfire exposure, specify its defensible-space actions, and write its trigger-based leave plan.
bands.11–12: Write the leave plan for a street, with triggers, routes and who checks on whom, and present it to residents or a role-played council.

themes.description: Re-entry dangers, insurance documentation, and the recovery sequence for a household that just lost its rooms.
themes.transfer_check: Produce the first-72-hours checklist for a post-fire household — safety, claims evidence, shelter, records — from a case study.

bands.K–2: Learn that after a fire you do not go back inside until a grown-up says it is safe.
bands.3–5: Make a list of what a family needs in the first days after a fire — somewhere to sleep, clothes, the important papers.
bands.6–8: Produce a first-days checklist for a post-fire household from a case study — safety, records, shelter — in the order it is needed.
bands.9–10: Produce the first-72-hours checklist for a post-fire household — safety, claims evidence, shelter, records — from a case study.
bands.11–12: Write the recovery plan for a post-fire household through the first month, including the insurance evidence sequence and the support agencies.

themes.theme: Fire and the very young and very old
themes.description: Who dies in home fires and why — mobility, hearing, medication sleep — and adapting alarms, plans and drills to real occupants.
themes.transfer_check: Adapt a real dwelling's fire plan for a named occupant with impaired mobility, hearing or cognition, and test the adaptation.

bands.K–2: Practise waking a sleeping grown-up by shouting and shaking when the alarm sounds.
bands.3–5: Think of someone who could not hear or move fast in a fire, and say how you would help them get out.
bands.6–8: Adapt your home's fire plan for a named person with impaired hearing, mobility or memory, and test the adaptation once.
bands.9–10: Adapt a real dwelling's fire plan for a named occupant with impaired mobility, hearing or cognition, and test the adaptation.
bands.11–12: Adapt and drill the plan for a care setting or multi-occupant home, and write the staff card that says who moves whom, in what order.

themes.theme: Being the workplace or venue warden
themes.description: Sweep duties, refuge points, roll calls and the authority a high-vis vest carries when everyone else is deciding to finish their coffee.
themes.transfer_check: Act as warden in a real or staged evacuation: complete the sweep, manage the reluctant, and deliver the roll-call report.

bands.K–2: Practise being the line leader who counts everyone at the meeting place.
bands.3–5: Be the drill helper who checks the room is empty and reports to the teacher at the assembly point.
bands.6–8: Act as warden in a staged evacuation: sweep the area, move the slow, and give the roll-call report.
bands.9–10: Act as warden in a real or staged evacuation: complete the sweep, manage the reluctant, and deliver the roll-call report.
bands.11–12: Plan and run the evacuation for a venue with a public audience, brief the wardens, and deliver the report the fire service would ask for.

tracks.name: When the ground, water or sky turns

themes.description: Flash versus river flood, the depths that move cars and people, and the property-level defences that actually help.
themes.transfer_check: Read your address's flood risk from official maps, and state the action sequence for a warning at each of three lead times.

bands.K–2: Learn the rule for moving water — never walk or ride into it — and where the family goes when the water comes.
bands.3–5: Find your home on a flood map with help, and say what you would take upstairs first.
bands.6–8: Read your address's flood risk from official maps and state what you do for a warning with a day, an hour, and minutes to go.
bands.9–10: Read your address's flood risk from official maps, and state the action sequence for a warning at each of three lead times.
bands.11–12: Write the flood plan for a household with a ground-floor bedroom and a car, with the three lead times, and test the property-level defences named.

themes.description: What wind speeds do to roofs, trees and driving, the pre-storm hour list, and the shelter spots inside a home.
themes.transfer_check: Complete a real pre-storm property walk-around — securing, clearing, charging — and identify the safest internal refuge with reasons.

bands.K–2: Help bring the toys and garden things inside before a storm, and learn the safest room in the house.
bands.3–5: Help with the pre-storm walk-around — chairs in, bins tied, torches charged — and show the family the inside room away from windows.
bands.6–8: Do a real pre-storm property walk-around — securing, clearing, charging — and pick the safest internal refuge with reasons.
bands.9–10: Complete a real pre-storm property walk-around — securing, clearing, charging — and identify the safest internal refuge with reasons.
bands.11–12: Write the storm checklist for a building with several households, run the walk-around with them, and decide when the roof means leaving instead of sheltering.

themes.description: What buildings do in shaking, the myths (doorways, running out), and the aftershock rules.
themes.transfer_check: Run the full drop-cover-hold drill in two different rooms, then perform the post-shake checks — gas, structure, exits — in order.

bands.K–2: Practise drop, cover and hold on under the table until the count ends.
bands.3–5: Practise drop, cover and hold on in two rooms, and name the myths — doorways, running outside — that are not safe.
bands.6–8: Run the full drop-cover-hold drill in two rooms, then do the after-shake checks — gas, structure, exits — in order.
bands.9–10: Run the full drop-cover-hold drill in two different rooms, then perform the post-shake checks — gas, structure, exits — in order.
bands.11–12: Lead the drill for a group, run the post-shake checks on a building, and decide whether it can be re-entered or must be evacuated, with reasons.

themes.description: Heatwave physiology, the rooms and hours that matter, and the neighbours on the checking list.

bands.9–10: Write and rehearse a heatwave plan for a real household including one vulnerable person's specific arrangements.
bands.11–12: Write the heatwave checking rota for a street or building, including the signs that mean calling for help, and run the first day of it.

themes.theme: Cold, snow and the iced-in week
themes.description: Freezing pipes, stranded cars, carbon monoxide from improvised heating — the winter emergency's specific traps.

bands.9–10: Prepare a real car and home for a cold snap against a checklist, including the in-car survival kit demonstrated.
bands.11–12: Plan the cold-snap response for a household with an older person and no backup heat, including the carbon-monoxide rules and the moment to relocate them.

themes.description: Where lightning actually strikes people, the timing rules, and the safe and unsafe shelters.
themes.transfer_check: Given three outdoor scenarios with a building storm, state and justify the correct action and shelter for each.

themes.theme: Landslip, sinkhole and the moving ground
themes.description: Reading slopes and warning signs — cracks, leaning trees, sudden springs — and who to call before the road drops.

themes.description: The overturned tanker, the chemical smell, the plume — shelter-in-place done properly versus the instinct to drive through it.
themes.transfer_check: Demonstrate full shelter-in-place for a staged airborne release — sealing, ventilation off, information channel on — in your own home.

bands.6–8: Demonstrate full shelter-in-place for a staged airborne release in your own home — sealing, ventilation off, information channel on.
bands.9–10: Demonstrate full shelter-in-place for a staged airborne release — sealing, ventilation off, information channel on — in your own home.
bands.11–12: Run shelter-in-place for a school or workplace, including the decision to end it, and write the notice that tells people what to do next.

themes.theme: Warnings and the words they use

bands.6–8: Match your region's alert levels to the actions each demands and show where the warnings arrive on your own devices, tested.
bands.9–10: Match your region's actual alert levels to required actions, and show where the warnings arrive on your own devices, tested.

themes.description: Routes, timing, the full tank rule, and the decision discipline that leaves before the road jams.
themes.transfer_check: Plan two evacuation routes from your home to defined refuges, drive or trace both, and state your pre-committed leave triggers.

bands.6–8: Plan two evacuation routes from home to defined refuges, drive or trace both, and set the triggers that mean leaving early.

themes.description: Emergency services, civil protection, utilities, charities — who does what in a disaster and where the citizen fits.
themes.transfer_check: Map the actual response structure for your area — agencies, roles, activation — and identify the citizen-facing entry point of each.

themes.description: Why untasked helpers clog disasters, and the registered, trained routes by which help actually helps.

bands.9–10: Identify and complete registration (or its full application) with one recognised local response or resilience group.
bands.11–12: Register with a group, complete its first training, and write the guide that tells untrained helpers where to go instead of the scene.

themes.description: Look, listen, link — steadying frightened people without therapy or platitudes, and the referrals beyond your role.

bands.11–12: Deliver psychological first aid in a staged mass event, keep to your role, and teach the look-listen-link method to new helpers.

themes.description: Running the hall where evacuees arrive: registration, needs triage, families kept together, and the quiet corner that matters.

themes.description: Rumour dynamics in disasters, official channels, and being the neighbour who relays what is true rather than what is loud.

themes.description: Recording what happened — structures, utilities, needs — in the form responders and insurers can actually use.
